idiom_name: Dictionary<(int X, int Y), List<Entity>> of cell buckets
implementation_notes: The runtime has no spatial index, so the hand realization is a Dictionary<(int X, int Y), List<Entity>> keyed by cell coordinates (or a flat List<Entity>[] array for a bounded world); TryGetValue and List<T> provide every primitive. This remains the default for game loops that move many small entities per frame. When the indexed entities are physics bodies, prefer the Unity variant: the engine already maintains a broadphase and querying it avoids a second, divergent index.
pitfalls: Dictionary is not thread-safe: mutating cells from a job or physics callback while another thread queries requires confinement or a concurrent structure.
Empty cell lists are never reclaimed unless swept, so a world that is traversed once keeps one list per visited cell forever.
Value-tuple keys hide boxing-free hashing but still hash and compare per lookup; for very hot loops a flat array grid avoids the dictionary entirely.

variants.name: Unity physics broadphase queries
variants.implementation_notes: Unity's physics engine owns a broadphase over all colliders; Physics.OverlapSphereNonAlloc fills a caller-provided Collider[] buffer without allocating, and Unity Physics exposes OverlapAabb over CollisionWorld. No hand-written cells are needed as long as membership equals the physics world, which makes this the right realization for gameplay triggers and explosion queries. It replaces the classic structure only for colliders - logical entities that are not in the physics world (map pins, inventory slots) still need the bucket grid.
pitfalls: The broadphase reflects the last physics step unless synchronisation is enabled, so freshly moved objects can be found at their old positions.
Layer masks and trigger interaction decide membership: a collider outside the mask is invisible to the query even though it is nearby.
OverlapSphere allocates a new array per call; in per-frame code the NonAlloc form (or an OverlapAabb job) is required.
